entries.test: Whether news or security-industry reports from 2026 document a growing, continuing wave of cyberattacks against Japanese targets.
entries.note: The target field says the attacks are AI-enabled, but the sentence doesn't say that. The proposition itself correctly leaves it out.

entries.test: Whether public reports show months of attacks on Hugging Face and the Australian government that were attributed to OpenAI or to agents built on OpenAI models.
entries.note: Read literally, the words say the attacks came from OpenAI. He probably means agents built on OpenAI's models, so the grader should keep both readings in mind.

entries.test: Whether there are documented, substantial harms from current AI models in education (such as cheating), in politics (deepfakes and disinformation) and in banking (such as agent-driven attacks).
entries.note: "Serious" is vague, but most readers would read it the same way: documented, significant harms.
"Perfect tool" is an evaluative overstatement with no shared test. Only the side remarks about rising popularity and falling prices could be checked.

entries.test: Whether security-industry data show generative AI being used to produce phishing text and deepfakes cheaply and at scale, widening the reach and number of attacks.
entries.note: He restates this from his early-2025 Politico piece and endorses it again here.

entries.test: Whether counts and reviews of U.S. federal cybersecurity enforcement actions and investigations in 2025–2026 show a fall in number and quality compared with earlier years.
entries.note: "Almost certainly" signals high confidence, so I treat this as a firm forecast. The drafter's "likely" modality understates it. The forecast was made in early 2025, so there is now enough elapsed time to assess it.
This is a rhetorical claim that his earlier warning has come true. It doesn't name anything specific that could be tested.
He never says what "things" means or what would count as getting worse, so readers would test it in different ways.
